title: How Roller Derby Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore roller derby: its origins in the 1930s as a transcontinental skating endurance contest promoted by Leo Seltzer, the suggestion from sportswriter Damon Runyon to add contact, its popularity through the 1940s-50s, the 1970s televised revival and decline, the all-women flat track revival starting in Austin, Texas in 2001, the Women's Flat Track Derby Association (WFTDA), the rules and strategy (jammers, pivots, blockers, lead jammer, penalties and the sin bin), training, injuries, and the film Whip It. The episode also includes Josh's Atlanta Roller Girls plug, playoff schedules, and a long run of listener mail and fan gift thank-yous, plus a trivia event plug.

segments.title: Opening banter and roller derby playoff season
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then Josh notes the current roller derby playoff season and the revival's visibility, mentions the Atlanta Roller Girls, and the Dutch Land Rollers logo.

segments.title: 1930s origins: transcontinental endurance skate
segments.summary: Leo Seltzer's transcontinental roller skating endurance contest, its boredom, and Damon Runyon's suggestion to add contact that led to roller derby.

segments.title: Growth, 1970s decline and televised revival
segments.summary: Roller derby's popularity in the 1940s and 1950s, decline in the 1970s amid economic trouble, televised 1970s matches with colorful announcers, and an artificial touring revival that drifted into staged fighting.

segments.title: Co-ed origins and the all-women revival
segments.summary: Early teams were co-ed while periods were gender-separated; the modern revival is all women, starting in Austin, Texas in 2001, and the Women's Flat Track Derby Association formed in 2004. Flat track versus banked tracks is discussed, and the documentary Hell on Wheels and the film Whip It are mentioned.

segments.title: Team names, costumes and the spirit of the sport
segments.summary: Skaters adopt fun names and costumes, and the hosts point out that body size matters less than skill. Debbie's skater names and the New York team's theme are mentioned.

segments.title: Training and skills
segments.summary: Training includes calisthenics, falling and rolling, jumping, stopping and high-speed skating; newer skaters are separated from veterans, and skaters must pass a test before sanctioned play. Debbie's experience is described.

segments.title: How the game is played: positions, jams and scoring
segments.summary: Two teams of five; jammers score points by passing opposing players after the first lap; pivots set pace and call plays; blockers keep the opposing jammer back. Jams last up to two minutes, and the lead jammer can end a jam.

segments.title: Blocking rules, penalties and the sin bin
segments.summary: Rules on blocking, including no extended arms, no elbows above shoulders, no blocks above mid-thigh, and no deliberate falls. Minor penalties send skaters to the sin bin; major infractions can remove a skater.

segments.title: Injuries, community, and playoff schedules
segments.summary: Injuries such as tailbone bruising and fishnet burn are discussed, skaters pay their own way, leagues are largely charitable and sponsored, and WFTDA playoff locations and dates are listed.

segments.title: Listener mail and fan gift thank-yous
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and contributors for gifts, including candies, books, a CD, a tick remover, a flower pen, and custom prints, and mention Facebook, Twitter, blog and an Atlanta trivia event.
